source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models (re-read PDF for gaps 1-2)
finding: MAI-DxO is compared to a baseline prompt only as a whole. Variants differ by budget, question-only and ensemble. There is no run that removes one persona (for example Dr. Challenger) and no run that matches tokens. The paper says inference cost ($0.15 per case) is negligible next to test cost, so compute was never optimised or matched.
numbers: Off-the-shelf o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO (no budget, o3) 81.9% at $4,735. Budgeted variant 79.9% at $2,396. Ensemble 85.5% at $7,184. Physicians (21, 764 diagnoses) 19.9% at $2,963. SDBench 304 NEJM cases; 56 held-out test cases. Gains significant for all models (p<0.005, one-sided paired permutation) except o3 and o4-mini, whose gain was in cost.
quote: MAI-DxO often sought disconfirming evidence and switched its diagnostic path
limits: Gap 1 and gap 2 stay open: the paper has no per-role ablation and no equal-token control. Ensemble is described as multiple independent no-budget runs plus a final aggregation panel, so ensemble gain mixes sampling and aggregation. Challenger value is shown only by hand-read cases.
agent_relevance: Treat the 3.3-point scaffold gain on o3 and the 'challenger reduces anchoring' story as unproven. Our own test must hold tokens equal and drop one role at a time.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis (ensemble, model-agnostic gains, held-out set)
finding: Scaffold gains were larger for weaker base models and small for reasoning models. The 56-case hidden test set (CPC 2024-2025) was used as a partial check on memorisation; most cases came after model training cutoffs. A single-turn vs batch ablation on MAI-DxO (o3) gave equal accuracy.
numbers: Single vs batched testing, test set only: 83.9% both; cost $3,991 single vs $5,084 batch. Authors say AI agents did better on the 56-case test subset than on all 304 cases. Worked example: o3 baseline fixated on antibiotic toxicity and paid $3,431 for a wrong answer; MAI-DxO asked about hand sanitiser first and paid $795 for a right one.
limits: Gap 6: no numeric pre-cutoff vs post-cutoff comparison is given, only the statement that the test cases are mostly outside training data and results held. Better test-set scores argue against, not for, memorisation inflating the 304-case numbers. Anchoring example is one case, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Scaffold value looks largest on weaker models. Do not expect a big accuracy gain on a frontier reasoner; expect cost savings and fewer anchored paths.

source: Towards a science of scaling agent systems (arXiv 2512.08296)
finding: First token-matched comparison I found of a single agent against four multi-agent architectures. Multi-agent help depended on the task. It helped when the task split into independent parts and hurt when steps were sequential. Not a medical study.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 9 models (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic), all matched at mean 4,800 reasoning tokens per trial. Finance Agent: centralised +80.8% (0.631 vs 0.349). PlanCraft: hybrid -39.1%, independent -70.0%. SWE-bench Verified: independent -14.9%. Mean multi-agent change -0.3% (95% CI -58.7% to +77.2%). Error amplification vs single agent: centralised 4.4, hybrid 5.1, decentralised 7.8, independent 17.2.
limits: Not diagnosis. Authors not captured from the fetch. Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read. Two different single-agent baselines are quoted for Finance Agent (0.349 and 0.280).
agent_relevance: Indirect answer to gap 1: at equal tokens, panel structure is not a free win. Diagnosis is sequential (each test depends on the last), the case where multi-agent hurt. Our challenger step should be tested against the same model given the same token budget.

source: Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate (arXiv 2502.08788)
finding: Abstract only. Five multi-agent debate methods, nine benchmarks and four models: debate often failed to beat chain-of-thought and self-consistency even with much more inference compute. Model heterogeneity is proposed as the fix.
numbers: 5 MAD methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 foundation models. No numbers on the page I read. No medical dataset named.
limits: Fetch returned the abstract page only; experiment tables not read. Author names not captured.
agent_relevance: Supports caution on gap 1: a debate-style panel from one base model should be benchmarked against self-consistency at equal tokens before we adopt it.

source: Kraidia et al. (2026) When collaboration fails: persuasion driven adversarial influence in multi agent LLM debate (Sci Rep)
finding: One agent that argues confidently and wrongly can pull a debate toward a wrong answer. More agents, more rounds, and simple prompt defences did not fix it. Best-of-N and RAG made flawed arguments look more credible.
numbers: Single adversary lowers system accuracy 10-40% and raises consensus on incorrect answers by over 30%.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Models and benchmarks not named there. Not a diagnosis study.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and gap 2 risk: a challenger role that argues is also a channel for a wrong, confident argument. A challenger must be tied to evidence checks, not to rhetoric.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: question-asking LLMs and a benchmark for reliable interactive clinical reasoning (arXiv 2406.00922)
finding: When models must elicit the case themselves, accuracy falls well below the full-information level. Naive question asking does not recover it. A confidence-gated abstention strategy recovers part of the gap.
numbers: iMedQA: GPT-4 full info 79.7%, initial info only 54.5%, no info 42.2%, basic interactive 55.4%, best interactive 66.1%. Llama-3-70b: 84.7 / 58.5 / 46.3 / 55.1 / 60.9. GPT-3.5: 55.8 / 45.6 / 36.7 / 42.2 / 50.2. iCraft-MD: GPT-4 91.4 / 67.9 / 43.6 / 73.6 / 84.3. Abstract claims +22.3% from abstention; I could not reproduce that figure from Table 2.
limits: MedQA-style and a small iCraft-MD set (about 140 items); GPT-4 and Llama-3 era, not o3 or later. Simulated patient is an LLM. Only first 100,000 characters read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly answered for GPT-4-class models: a loss of about 25 points from full to initial info, with 'ask when unsure' recovering about half. Our S-states for case elicitation should include a confidence gate before asking or answering.

source: Neurosurgery vignette-to-conversation study (2026) A multi-agent AI framework for interactive neurosurgical education and evaluation (Neurosurgery Practice 7(2))
finding: Turning 608 exam vignettes into patient-AI plus system-AI conversations cut GPT-4o accuracy sharply, most of all for free response. Giving the model an objective-data agent restored much of it.
numbers: Text cases (n=218), GPT-4o: multiple choice 89.0% vignette, 60.9% conversation (patient AI only), 67.4% with system AI. Free response 78.4%, 30.3%, 61.8%. Image cases (n=390): MC 68.7 / 48.8 / 49.7; FR 47.2 / 25.3 / 36.5. Residents (n=10, 8 questions) 70.0% vs GPT-4o 28.3% on free-response conversation (P=.003).
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one specialty, proprietary question bank, residents answered only 8 questions. Vignettes were not written for dialogue, so the patient AI often could not answer, which inflates the loss.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: strong evidence that a lossy simulated patient costs a frontier-era model 20-45 points. Part is simulator limits, so a clean test needs a patient simulator that can answer any question the source case supports.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) AgentClinic: a multimodal agent benchmark to evaluate AI in simulated clinical environments (arXiv 2405.07960)
finding: Sequential, agent-must-ask format gives much lower accuracy than static MedQA, and MedQA accuracy predicts it only weakly. Injected patient or doctor biases cost GPT-4 little. Tools helped some models.
numbers: AgentClinic-MedQA: Claude 3.5 62.1%, GPT-4 51.6%, GPT-4o 34.2%, human physicians 54% (N=20 interactions). MIMIC-IV: Claude 3.5 42.9%, GPT-4 34.0%. Interaction limit: N=10 gives 25%, N=20 gives 52%. GPT-4 under cognitive-bias prompts: patient bias to about 48%, doctor bias to about 50.3% from 52% unbiased (max drop 4 points, average 1.5). Mixtral 37% to about 29-35%. NEJM image set: Claude 3.5 37.2%, GPT-4 27.7%. No calibration results.
limits: Small N per cell; GPT-4 simulated patient; paper has internal inconsistencies (bias count 24 vs 23). Two different 'up to' figures for Llama-3 tool gain (92% vs 19.7%).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and gap 8: elicitation costs accuracy, and prompt-induced bias had small effect on GPT-4 but large effect on weaker models. Turn budget matters: more turns help until about 20.

source: Bean et al. (2025) Clinical knowledge in LLMs does not translate to human interactions (arXiv 2504.18919) - simulated users and failure analysis (re-read for gaps 3-4)
finding: Public participants lost most of the LLM's skill in the hand-off. Transcripts show users omitted key details and dropped correct suggestions. A GPT-4o simulated patient did better than real people and predicted human scores poorly.
numbers: N=1,298; 600 responses per arm. LLM alone: conditions 94.9%, disposition 56.3%. With participants: conditions at most 34.5%, disposition under 44.2%. Control: at least one relevant condition 47.0% (control odds 1.76 higher, CI 1.45-2.13); LLMs named a relevant condition in 65.7-73.2% of conversations; 2.21 conditions suggested per chat, 34.0% correct; users listed 1.33, 38.7% correct. Simulated users (300 chats): disposition 57.3%, conditions 60.7%; correlation with human scores weak (conditions about 0). Prompts were run separately for disposition and conditions because models ignored multiple-choice format when both were asked together.
limits: General public with vignettes, not clinicians; 2023-24 models (GPT-4o, Llama 3, Command R+). The cross-check could not verify the 43.0% control figure; this page shows 47.0% for conditions and 43.0% as an overall disposition rate.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a simulated patient overstates how well a model copes with real, lossy input. Gap 4: loss sits in the interface step (what the user types, what survives to the final answer), not only in model knowledge.

source: Siden et al. (2025) A typology of physician input approaches to using AI chatbots for clinical decision-making (npj Digit Med)
finding: Chat logs from two RCTs were coded into four input styles: copy-paster, selective copy-paster, summariser, searcher. No style was linked to higher case scores.
numbers: Two RCTs, four input types, linear mixed-effects model. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only (PMC12780094). Authors suggest prompting strategy, engagement and output interpretation matter more, but did not test them.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: how much case text goes in does not explain the human-plus-LLM failure. Output format and interpretation remain untested, so gap 4 stays open.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Human-LLM collaboration in clinical medicine: systematic review and meta-analysis (npj Digit Med 9:195)
finding: Pooled data on humans with an LLM versus humans alone are sparse and imprecise. Three-arm studies did not show human-plus-AI beating AI alone.
numbers: 10 peer-reviewed studies (3 preprints in sensitivity). Diagnostic accuracy (k=2): RR 1.59, 95% CI 0.08-32.74. Composite diagnostic/management score (k=2): +4.88 points, CI +0.65 to +9.12, prediction interval -31.65 to 41.42. Time (k=3): +0.4 min, CI -4.18 to 4.97, I2=70.1%. Factual error rate 26-36%.
limits: Abstract only (PMC12953916). Searches ran to 28 June 2025, so Qazi 2026 and later trials are probably not in it.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 and gap 4: pooled evidence for human-LLM benefit is weak and unstable. Do not design our agent on the assumption that a human downstream adds accuracy.

source: Goh et al. (2025) GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks (Nat Med 31:1233) - abstract re-read via Europe PMC
finding: Management-reasoning gain reconfirmed from the abstract. The LLM-assisted group did not differ from the LLM alone.
numbers: 92 physicians, 5 vignettes. LLM-assisted vs conventional: +6.5 points (95% CI 2.7-10.2, P<0.001). Time +119.3 s (CI 17.4-221.2, P=0.02). LLM-assisted vs LLM alone: -0.9 points (CI -9.0 to 7.2, P=0.8). Nov 2023-Apr 2024, NCT06208423. Erratum published (Nat Med 31:1370).
limits: Abstract only. Same research group as Goh 2024. An erratum exists; I did not check what it changed.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: this is the same trial, not a replication. The effect sits on management tasks where physicians had only conventional resources.

source: Replication search for Goh 2025: Lievin et al. (2026, Nature, AMIE disease management) and O'Sullivan et al. (2026, Nat Med, cardiology)
finding: Two later randomized studies of LLM management reasoning exist, but both test different systems and populations. Neither replicates the GPT-4 plus physicians design.
numbers: AMIE: blinded virtual OSCE, 100 multivisit scenarios, 21 PCPs, non-inferior to PCPs on management reasoning, better on treatment and investigation precision (no numbers in abstract). Cardiology: 9 cardiologists, AI-assisted responses preferred 46.7% vs 32.7% (P=0.02); clinically significant errors 13.1% vs 24.3% (P=0.033).
limits: Abstracts only via Europe PMC (PMC13421318 for AMIE). The AMIE study compares an AI alone with PCPs, not physicians using an LLM. No same-design replication was found in Europe PMC; arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: independent signals for management reasoning exist, none is a direct replication.

source: Qazi et al. (2026) Automation bias in LLM-assisted diagnostic reasoning among physicians trained in AI literacy (NEJM AI, doi 10.1056/aioa2501001)
finding: Physicians who saw planted wrong LLM advice scored lower. An accompanying editorial argues the drop looks like the general effect of wrong information on reasoning, not only automation bias.
numbers: 44 physicians (22 per arm), 264 diagnostic cases. Accuracy 73.3% with erroneous suggestions vs 84.9% control; adjusted -14.0 points (95% CI -18.9 to -9.1, P<0.0001). Top-choice 76.1% vs 90.5%, adjusted -18.3 (CI -26.6 to -10.0).
limits: Abstract only. Earlier line b24 gave the CI as -19.7 to -8.3; this record gives -18.9 to -9.1. Possible preprint-vs-final difference; unresolved. Single country, planted errors.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: humans anchor on flawed advice (-14 points). No agent version has been measured yet. The editorial's reading means a test needs a no-advice control and a wrong-advice control for an agent too.

source: Real-time AI diagnostic copilot in simulated primary care consultations (JMIR Form Res 2026, doi 10.2196/104579)
finding: Voice-based AI assistance raised top-3 diagnostic accuracy. Top-1 gain and over-reliance on a wrong suggestion were both not significant.
numbers: 13 physicians, 260 simulated consultations. Top-3: 62.3% vs 74.6% (adjusted OR 2.68, CI 1.24-6.12, P=.01; +12.3 points). Top-1: 47.8% vs 57% (AOR 1.83, CI 0.93-3.80, P=.08). Agreement with an incorrect suggestion: 38.8% unassisted vs 55.8% assisted (AOR 2.08, CI 0.89-5.19, P=.09). Consultation time +10.7%.
limits: Abstract only. Tiny physician sample, simulated patients. Unassisted arm was resource-restricted.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5: a short ranked list helped top-3 but not top-1. Weak support that a ranked, structured output can help humans, in contrast with Goh 2024 free-form chat use. Not a head-to-head of formats.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (npj Digit Med; arXiv 2402.08113) - BiasMedQA
finding: Bias-inducing prompt text cut accuracy for every model tested. GPT-4 was the most robust. Bias education and few-shot examples raised GPT-4 back up. Anchoring itself was not tested.
numbers: 1,273 MedQA items, 7 biases. GPT-4 no bias 72.7%; false consensus 62.5%; frequency 62.7%; confirmation 72.5%. GPT-3.5 49.7% to 23.9-40.7%. Mixtral 51.8% to 37.3-49.7%. Llama-2-70B 35.7% to 10.4-20.7%. GPT-4 mean biased accuracy 67.3% none, 70.9% education, 73.1% one-shot, 74.9% few-shot. Average effect: false consensus 24.9%, frequency 18.2%, recency 12.9%, confirmation 8.1%.
limits: Multiple-choice exam items, 2023 models. PaLM-2 excluded from one-shot and few-shot (94-99% non-response). Anchoring and premature closure not among the seven.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and gap 9: wrong framing text in context hurts weaker models a lot and GPT-4 less; a short debiasing instruction recovers part. A test on current models with a planted wrong hypothesis is still needed.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA (BMJ Digit Health AI)
finding: Reasoning-enhanced models were more accurate on average but did not become reliably less biased. Debiasing and few-shot prompts helped all three models.
numbers: 1,273 vignettes, 7 biases. Llama-3.3-70B reasoning 72.5-82.1% vs base 61.0-73.4%. Qwen3-32B 71.7-78.7% vs 55.5-64.1%. Gemini-2.5-Flash 81.8-88.6% vs 80.0-83.7%; on four unpublished bias prompts it fell to 47.4-86.1%, which the authors read as contamination or brittleness. Reasoning raised vulnerability to several biases in Llama and Gemini.
limits: Abstract only (PMC13528315). Small open and mid-size models, multiple-choice items.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and 9: a thinking model is not protected from planted bias; an explicit debiasing or challenger instruction still helped. Supports keeping a challenger step even on reasoning models.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Development of a framework for evaluating LLM safety and reliability (J Med Syst 50:136)
finding: On hard emergency cases, anchoring-bias failures and rare-disease misses varied widely between six current models. Most dangerous outputs were random, not systematic.
numbers: 54 non-public emergency cases, 6 LLMs, 3 queries each, 972 physician-scored responses (Aug-Dec 2025). Anchoring-bias failure (score <=3): 6.9-26.4%. Rare-disease recognition 6.1-37.9%. Catastrophic failure 1.5% for the two safest vs 6.0% for the rest (p<0.001). 31 of 34 dangerous combinations were stochastic. GPT-5.1 least reproducible (within-case SD 2.69).
limits: Abstract only (PMC13601161). Single centre, proof of concept. Only three of six models named in the record.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: first measured anchoring-failure rates for current models (up to a quarter of cases), and a strong case for repeat sampling to catch stochastic failures.

source: Griot et al. (2025) Large language models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning (Nat Commun 16; MetaMedQA)
finding: Twelve models answered confidently even when no option was correct. Confidence carried some signal for the three models that varied it. Almost none could say 'I don't know'.
numbers: 1,373 six-option questions (MedQA base, plus fictional Glianorex, malformed and modified items). GPT-4o accuracy 73.3%; confidence 5 gave 83.2%, 3-4 gave 45.9%, under 3 gave 16.7%. Qwen2-72B 77.9% at high confidence vs 59.3% medium. GPT-3.5 56.9% vs 44.8%. Nine other models nearly always said 5. Missing-answer recall GPT-4o 46.1%, GPT-3.5 11.3%. Unknown recall: 9 of 12 models 0%, GPT-4o 3.7%. A full role prompt raised GPT-4o to 78.8% accuracy (p=0.0009) and unknown recall to 51.8%.
limits: Multiple choice, 2024 models; not open diagnosis and not CPC. Paper does not report mean confidence for right vs wrong answers. Verbalised confidence only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: verbalised confidence is informative for GPT-4o-class models but compressed near the top and absent from smaller ones. Do not use it alone as a stopping signal; no CPC top-1 calibration test exists.

source: Oral autoimmune blistering disease multimodal LLM study (Diagnostics 2026, doi 10.3390/diagnostics16172761)
finding: Two current multimodal models differed in calibration even though both were accurate: the more accurate one was worse calibrated.
numbers: 200 confirmed cases, 4 diseases. Claude Opus 4.7 accuracy 92.0% vs Gemini Pro 3 86.0% (p=0.012). Brier 0.0468 vs 0.0558 (Claude better). Expected calibration error 0.251 vs 0.083 (Gemini better).
limits: Abstract only. Image classification into four diseases, not open differential. Model names as given in the record.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: accuracy and calibration can come apart in current models, so confidence needs its own measurement on our cases.

source: Conditional perplexity scoring for LLM-generated differential diagnoses (JMIR Form Res 2026, doi 10.2196/98819)
finding: A cheap reranking signal (how likely a small model finds each candidate diagnosis given the case) separated correct from incorrect candidates only moderately. It did not reliably put the right diagnosis above the strongest wrong one.
numbers: 392 case reports (Am J Case Reports, 2022); differential lists from LLaMA2, Bard, GPT-4; scorer Qwen2.5-1.5B. 823 correct vs 10,875 incorrect candidates. AUC 0.666 (CI 0.644-0.689); GPT-4 lists 0.678. Correct beat the mean incorrect candidate in 88.1-91.1% of lists.
limits: Abstract only (PMC13557325). Old generators, tiny scorer, case reports not CPCs. Authors call it preliminary.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: only direct rerank test found. A weak reranker does not close a top-1 vs top-10 gap. An LLM discriminator with evidence checks is untested on CPCs.

source: Search note for gaps 5, 6 and 9 (Europe PMC, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, 1 Nov 2026)
finding: Negative result. No study was found that compares diagnostic accuracy on cases published before and after a model cutoff, that adds a rerank or discrimination stage to CPC top-1, or that retests forced-differential or Bayesian prompts on current reasoning models. Savage 2024 and the 2026 BiasMedQA debiasing result remain the only prompt-format evidence.
numbers: WebSearch quota was exhausted. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429. Only Europe PMC and direct page fetches worked. Queries on pre/post cutoff, top-1 reranking, and MAI-DxO reproductions returned no matching study (one nursing-scenario paper evaluated MAI-DxO, 110 nurses, no numbers).
limits: Absence of evidence here reflects the limited search path, not proof of absence. arXiv-only work would not appear in Europe PMC.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5, 6 and 9 stay open and should be retried when search quota returns.
